ideas.hypothesis: Census tracts around MARTA stations with large joint-development TOD projects such as Lindbergh Center saw larger losses of low- and moderate-income households than tracts around stations without joint development, unless equity provisions like affordable-housing set-asides were attached.

sources.role: setting: MARTA's large-scale joint development at Lindbergh Center financed by converting capital assets
mechanism and measure: TOD can disrupt LMI neighborhoods; equity provisions in Denver, Fruitvale and Longfellow can mitigate

ideas.test: Difference-in-differences across MARTA station-area tracts using decennial census and ACS data (2000 vs 2015) on LMI household share, renter share and rent burden, comparing joint-development stations with and without affordability provisions to non-TOD stations.
ideas.disconfirming: LMI household share changes do not differ between joint-development and other station areas, or equity provisions make no difference.

ideas.hypothesis: Within transit station areas, higher pedestrian-friendliness (intersection density, sidewalk coverage, short blocks) explains most of the transportation cost advantage of TOD over transit-adjacent development, including in suburban settings.

sources.role: setting and mechanism: TOD as dense, pedestrian-friendly communities, examined in suburbs
finding and measure: TOD beats TAD on transportation affordability

ideas.test: Sample station areas classified as TOD or TAD; compute a walkability index from street-network and sidewalk data; take household transportation cost estimates (e.g. H+T-style data); regress costs on TOD status with and without the walkability index, separately for suburban stations.
ideas.disconfirming: The TOD-TAD cost gap remains unchanged after controlling for walkability, or walkability is unrelated to transportation costs in suburbs.

ideas.hypothesis: Applying Boston's typology-based TOD site selection criteria to MARTA stations would correctly identify the stations that later attracted the most TOD investment, showing the criteria transfer from dense older cities to a lower-density Sun Belt system.

sources.role: method: criteria for selecting promising TOD sites and classifying them into typologies
setting: MARTA's active TOD program and the Lindbergh Center case

ideas.test: Score all MARTA stations circa 2000 on the Boston criteria using land-use, parcel and ridership data; compare scores with subsequent permitted square footage within half a mile through 2015 using rank correlation.
ideas.disconfirming: Boston-criteria scores show no positive correlation with later TOD investment around MARTA stations.

ideas.hypothesis: In dense urban areas, the transit technology chosen (metro, light rail, BRT) matters less for station-area TOD intensity than site typology, whereas in growing mid-sized cities like Zhongshan technology choice strongly predicts subsequent development density.

sources.role: method: TOD site typologies for dense, older cities
setting: mass transit system design in a growing Chinese city applying updated technology

ideas.test: Cross-sectional comparison of station areas in a dense older city and a mid-sized growing city; outcome is change in floor-area ratio within 800 m; predictors are mode technology and typology, with an interaction for city type.
ideas.disconfirming: Technology effect on station-area density is the same in both city types, or typology fails to predict density in the dense city.

ideas.hypothesis: Evaluations of infill TOD financing tools give systematically more favourable results in case-study designs than in quasi-experimental designs with matched comparison sites.

sources.role: setting: financing strategies for TOD drawn from infill, brownfield and mixed-use examples, mainly case studies
mechanism: changes in economics research methods and technology shifting what counts as evidence

ideas.test: Systematic review of studies on infill and TOD financing tools (tax increment, joint development, TOD funds); code design type and reported effect direction; estimate whether case-study designs report positive effects more often.
ideas.disconfirming: The share of favourable findings does not differ by study design.

ideas.hypothesis: Regional-scale TOD studies that use spatial econometric methods find smaller station-area effects on development and ridership than single-site studies, because they account for development shifted from elsewhere in the region.

sources.role: setting: scaling new urbanism and TOD up to a regional strategy
mechanism: evolution of economics methods driven by technology and new tools

ideas.test: Re-estimate station-area development effects for one region with both a naive station-vs-nonstation comparison and a spatial model with spillover terms, using parcel permit data; compare effect sizes.
ideas.disconfirming: Spatial models produce effect sizes equal to or larger than naive single-site comparisons.

ideas.hypothesis: TOD in regions with lop-sided development, where growth is concentrated in a few nodes, produces more displacement of low-income residents than TOD in regions with more balanced growth.

sources.role: mechanism: Issawi's concept of lop-sided development, uneven sectoral and spatial growth
measure and finding: TOD can disrupt LMI neighborhoods; equity tools as moderators

ideas.test: Across several US metropolitan areas, compute a regional employment concentration index; measure LMI household loss around new stations from census data; regress displacement on concentration with station-level controls.
ideas.disconfirming: Regional development concentration is unrelated to station-area LMI losses.

ideas.hypothesis: TOD design features (mixed uses, reduced parking, walkable core) raise local business formation more in lagging neighborhoods than in already prosperous ones, reducing intra-urban lop-sided development.

sources.role: mechanism: lop-sided development and its correction
measure: list of TOD design ingredients from California case studies

ideas.test: Code TOD design features for California station areas from the case-study database; use business establishment counts before and after; test interaction of design score with baseline neighborhood income.
ideas.disconfirming: Design features increase business formation equally or more in prosperous neighborhoods.

ideas.hypothesis: Regions where TOD research and pilots are funded by government-industry consortiums deliver regional-scale TOD strategies faster than regions relying on local agency funding alone.

sources.role: mechanism: consortium vs high-level government funding as determinant of research and deployment progress
setting: turning TOD into a regional strategy

ideas.test: Compile a sample of metropolitan regions; code funding source for TOD research and pilots and the year a regional TOD policy was adopted; survival analysis of time to adoption.
ideas.disconfirming: Funding source shows no association with time to regional TOD policy adoption.

ideas.hypothesis: Availability of operating and performance data from funded demonstration projects increases the number of TOD design features actually implemented, since agencies can include them in alternatives analysis.

sources.role: mechanism: lack of operational data limits consideration in alternatives analysis; funding needed for full-scale tests
measure: TOD design ingredients and a funded case-study database

ideas.test: Compare TOD projects in California before and after the state-funded TOD case database was available, counting design features implemented per project; control for project size and city.
ideas.disconfirming: No increase in implemented design features after the funded data resource became available.
